name: Ahinoam
title: David's wife from Jezreel
summary: Ahinoam from Jezreel in Judah was among the first women David married, during the turbulent period when he lived as a fugitive fleeing Saul's persecution. She and Abigail shared David's wandering life and followed him all the way into Philistine territory, where they settled in Ziklag. When the Amalekites raided the city and carried off all its inhabitants, Ahinoam was taken captive—but David launched a bold rescue mission and brought everyone back to safety. After David was crowned king in Hebron, Ahinoam bore his firstborn son, Amnon. Amnon's fate—his abuse of his half-sister Tamar and the subsequent revenge by Absalom—testifies to the deep tensions and human costs within the rival dynastic network that grew up in David's household.

keyEvents.title: Marriage to David
keyEvents.description: Ahinoam from Jezreel became David's wife while he was fleeing from Saul. She is mentioned alongside Abigail as one of David's first two wives.

keyEvents.title: Followed David into exile
keyEvents.description: Ahinoam accompanied David to the land of the Philistines when he sought refuge with King Achish in Gath.

keyEvents.title: Captured by the Amalekites
keyEvents.description: While David and his men were away, the Amalekites attacked Ziklag and took Ahinoam and Abigail captive along with all the other women and children.

keyEvents.title: Saved from the Amalekites
keyEvents.description: David pursued the Amalekites and rescued Ahinoam and Abigail, along with everything that had been taken. No one was missing, neither small nor great.

keyEvents.title: Mother of Amnon in Hebron
keyEvents.description: In Hebron, Ahinoam gave birth to Amnon, who became David's firstborn son. Amnon is listed first among the sons born to David in Hebron.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy in Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Ahinoam is mentioned as the mother of Amnon, David's firstborn, in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chronicles.

versions.title: David's wife from Jezreel
versions.reason: [minor] The role of 'matriarch' is somewhat exaggerated for Ahinoam. She is primarily referred to as 'wife' and 'mother' in the biblical text, without the prominent role usually associated with the term 'matriarch' (Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel, Leah). 'David's wife' or 'royal wife' would have been more precise.; [minor] The summary is well formulated, but it could also mention that she accompanied David to Hebron where she gave birth to Amnon, in order to provide a more complete picture of her life story.; [major] Footnotes are missing. Information should be added about the meaning of the name, the confusion with Saul's wife Ahinoam (1 Sam 14:50), and the geographical and historical significance of Jezreel.; [minor] 1 Sam 30:5 specifically mentions Ahinoam and Abigail by name as the two who were taken captive. It is positive that this verse is included, but verse 4 deals primarily with David and his men weeping, and is less directly relevant to the actual event of captivity.

versions.summary: Ahinoam was a woman from Jezreel in Judah who became David's wife during the time he lived as an outlaw and fled from King Saul. Together with Abigail, she shared David's wandering life, including his stay in Philistine territory. When the Amalekites raided Ziklag and took all the women and children captive, Ahinoam was among those captured—but David struck back and rescued everyone. After Saul's death and David's coronation in Hebron, she gave birth to Amnon, the king's firstborn son. Amnon's later assault on his half-sister Tamar and his violent death (2 Sam 13) cast a dark light over the rivalry and unrest that characterized David's large and complex household.

footnotes.text: The name Ahinoam (Hebrew: אֲחִינֹעַם, Achinoam) means 'my brother is pleasant' or 'my brother is grace'. It is composed of אָח (ach, 'brother') and נֹעַם (noam, 'grace, pleasantness').

There are two women named Ahinoam in the Bible: Ahinoam from Jezreel, David's wife, and Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, who was King Saul's wife (1 Sam 14:50). A minority of scholars have speculated whether these could be the same person—that David took Saul's wife—but this is debated and lacks solid textual support.

Jezreel (Hebrew: יִזְרְעֶאל, 'God sows') was a city in the tribe of Judah (Josh 15:56), not to be confused with the more well-known Jezreel Valley in the north. The fact that Ahinoam came from this city in the Judah region fits well with David's presence in that area during his flight from Saul.

The fact that Amnon, Ahinoam's son, was David's firstborn initially gave him a strong position regarding inheritance rights. His assault on his half-sister Tamar and the subsequent murder at Absalom's hand (2 Sam 13) illustrate the destructive tensions that could arise in a polygamous royal household.

Ziklag, the city where Ahinoam was captured, was a Philistine city that King Achish of Gath gave to David as his base. Archaeological excavations have identified several possible locations for Ziklag, including Tell esh-Sharia (Tel Sera) and Khirbet el-Rai, but its exact location remains debated.

Polygamy was widespread among kings in the ancient Middle East, and David's marriages to Ahinoam and Abigail likely also served political purposes—forming alliances with influential clans in Judah. Ahinoam is consistently mentioned before Abigail in the texts, which may indicate that she was the first of the two wives.
